hints: The velocity function must be continuous at $t = 4$.
Substitute $t = 4$ into $v(t) = 5t^2 - 10t$ to evaluate the constant velocity $k$.
walkthrough:
By continuity of velocity across the transition at $t = 4$, equate $v(4)$ to $k$:
$$k = v(4) = 5(4)^2 - 10(4) = 5(16) - 40 = 80 - 40 = 40$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Velocity must be continuous at the transition time $t = 4$. This means the quadratic speed formula evaluated at $t = 4$ must equal the constant speed $k$:
$$k = v(4)$$

hints: For $0 \le t \le 4$, sketch the parabolic curve $v = 5t^2 - 10t$: it passes through $(0,0)$, reaches vertex at $t=1$ ($v=-5$), crosses axis at $t=2$, and rises to $(4,40)$.
For $4 \le t \le 14$, draw a horizontal line segment at constant velocity $v = 40$.
For $14 \le t \le 20$, draw a straight line with negative slope connecting $(14,40)$ to $(20,28)$.
walkthrough: For the first stage $0 \le t \le 4$: sketch the parabola $v(t) = 5t(t - 2)$. It starts at the origin $(0, 0)$, dips below the $t$-axis to a minimum of $v = -5$ at $t = 1$, crosses back through the $t$-axis at $t = 2$, and reaches $(4, 40)$.
For the second stage $4 \le t \le 14$: draw a horizontal line segment representing constant speed $v = 40$ from $t = 4$ to $t = 14$.
For the third stage $14 \le t \le 20$: draw a straight line with negative gradient connecting $(14, 40)$ to the final point $(20, 28)$.

teacher_walkthrough: For Stage 1 ($0 \le t \le 4$): sketch the parabola $v(t) = 5t^2 - 10t = 5t(t - 2)$. It starts at $(0,0)$, dips below the axis to a minimum of $-5$ at $t = 1$, crosses the time axis at $(2,0)$, and rises to $(4, 40)$.
For Stage 2 ($4 \le t \le 14$): draw a horizontal line segment from $(4, 40)$ to $(14, 40)$ representing constant velocity at $v = 40$.
For Stage 3 ($14 \le t \le 20$): draw a straight line with constant negative gradient connecting $(14, 40)$ to $(20, 28)$.

hints: Set $a(t) > 0$ and solve for $t$ within the valid interval $0 \le t \le 4$.
Verify that acceleration is zero for $4 < t < 14$ and negative for $14 < t < 20$.
walkthrough:
Differentiate the velocity function with respect to time to obtain acceleration for $0 \le t \le 4$:
$$a(t) = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(5t^2 - 10t) = 10t - 10$$

Impose the condition for positive acceleration ($a(t) > 0$):
$$10t - 10 > 0 \implies 10t > 10 \implies t > 1$$

Examine the remaining intervals: on $4 < t < 14$, $v$ is constant so $a = 0$; on $14 < t < 20$, $v$ decreases linearly so $a < 0$. Therefore, acceleration is positive strictly for:
$$1 < t \le 4$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Acceleration is the time derivative of velocity ($a = \frac{dv}{dt}$). Differentiate $v(t) = 5t^2 - 10t$ using the power rule:
$$a(t) = \frac{d}{dt}(5t^2 - 10t) = 2(5)t^{2-1} - 10 = 10t - 10$$

We want acceleration to be positive ($a(t) > 0$):
$$10t - 10 > 0$$

Add 10 to both sides and divide by 10 to solve the inequality:
$$10t > 10 \implies t > 1$$

Check the remaining intervals: for $4 < t < 14$, velocity is constant so $a = 0$; for $14 < t < 20$, velocity decreases so acceleration is negative ($-2\text{ m s}^{-2}$). Therefore, positive acceleration occurs only for $1 < t \le 4$.

hints: Velocity changes sign at $t = 2$. Separate the distance on $0 \le t \le 4$ into $\left|\int_0^2 v\,dt\right|$ and $\int_2^4 v\,dt$.
For $4 \le t \le 20$, compute the area of the rectangle ($4 \le t \le 14$) and the trapezium ($14 \le t \le 20$), then sum all areas.
walkthrough:
Recognize that total distance requires the sum of absolute areas because $v(t) < 0$ on $0 \le t < 2$ and $v(t) > 0$ on $2 < t \le 4$. Integrate $v(t) = 5t^2 - 10t$:
$$\int (5t^2 - 10t)\,dt = \frac{5}{3}t^3 - 5t^2$$

Calculate the distance travelled backwards in the first 2 seconds ($0 \le t \le 2$):
$$s_1 = \left|\left[\frac{5}{3}t^3 - 5t^2\right]_0^2\right| = \left|\frac{40}{3} - 20\right| = \left|-\frac{20}{3}\right| = \frac{20}{3}\text{ m}$$

Calculate the distance travelled forwards from $t = 2$ to $t = 4$:
$$s_2 = \left[\frac{5}{3}t^3 - 5t^2\right]_2^4 = \left(\frac{320}{3} - 80\right) - \left(-\frac{20}{3}\right) = \frac{80}{3} + \frac{20}{3} = \frac{100}{3}\text{ m}$$

Calculate the distance for $4 \le t \le 20$ from the geometric areas of the velocity-time graph:
For the rectangular section ($4 \le t \le 14$):
$$s_3 = 40 \times (14 - 4) = 400\text{ m}$$
For the trapezoidal section ($14 \le t \le 20$):
$$s_4 = \frac{1}{2}(40 + 28) \times (20 - 14) = \frac{1}{2}(68)(6) = 204\text{ m}$$

Sum all four individual distance components to obtain the total distance travelled:
$$d_{\text{total}} = s_1 + s_2 + s_3 + s_4 = \frac{20}{3} + \frac{100}{3} + 400 + 204 = 40 + 400 + 204 = 644\text{ m}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Notice that on the interval $0 \le t \le 2$, velocity is negative ($v < 0$), meaning the particle moves backwards. Total distance requires taking the absolute value of backward displacement plus forward displacement:
$$d = |s_1| + s_2 + s_3 + s_4$$

Calculate the backward displacement by integrating $5t^2 - 10t$ from $t = 0$ to $t = 2$:
$$s_1 = \left[\frac{5}{3}t^3 - 5t^2\right]_0^2 = \left(\frac{5}{3}(8) - 5(4)\right) - 0 = \frac{40}{3} - 20 = -\frac{20}{3}\text{ m} \implies |s_1| = \frac{20}{3}\text{ m}$$

Calculate the forward displacement by integrating from $t = 2$ to $t = 4$:
$$s_2 = \left[\frac{5}{3}t^3 - 5t^2\right]_2^4 = \left(\frac{5}{3}(64) - 5(16)\right) - \left(-\frac{20}{3}\right) = \left(\frac{320}{3} - 80\right) + \frac{20}{3} = \frac{80}{3} + \frac{20}{3} = \frac{100}{3}\text{ m}$$

Calculate the distance from $t = 4$ to $t = 14$ as the area of a rectangle ($10\text{ s} \times 40\text{ m/s}$):
$$s_3 = 10 \times 40 = 400\text{ m}$$

Calculate the distance from $t = 14$ to $t = 20$ as the area of a trapezium with parallel heights 40 and 28 over width 6:
$$s_4 = \frac{1}{2}(40 + 28) \times 6 = \frac{68}{2} \times 6 = 34 \times 6 = 204\text{ m}$$

Add all four distances together to find the total distance travelled:
$$d_{\text{total}} = \frac{20}{3} + \frac{100}{3} + 400 + 204 = \frac{120}{3} + 400 + 204 = 40 + 400 + 204 = 644\text{ meters}$$
